Promoting Electric Propulsion (2025) | Unmanned Division 1
Rapid 3D: AnElectric Vessel Engineered by the Robotics Club of Central Florida
Brandon Zhang, Caicheng Li, Dwight Howard II, James Dylan Kaney, Lee Marshall, Oli Marquez
Valenzuela, Matthew Barrs, and Michael LePrell
Robotics Club of Central Florida at the University of Central Florida
March 25, 2025
Figure 1: A picture of the RCCF PEP25 team. Due to various scheduling conflicts only (from left to right)
Matthew Barrs, Caicheng Li, and Dwight Howard II were able to show up for the picture.Rapid 3D: A 3D Printed Vessel 2

Abstract
Whether one is prototyping, recreating, or even creating a new unique item there is no question
that 3D printing is a positively helpful tool in the process of an item going from a fantastical idea to
reality. The Robotics Club of Central Florida (RCCF) has found 3D printing an essential part of bringing
forth an idea to the real world; however, this process is not without its challenges. With this paper,
RCCF’s Rapid 3D team presents the challenges of designing, developing, and testing a fully custom 3D
printed hull designed around a central direct drive electric propulsion system. This system is based upon
RCCF’s direct expertise in robotics, specifically the need to keep component interactions simple,
functional, and reliable. With that in mind, the drive assembly of the boat (Rapid 3D) features an
optimized propeller, selected based on diameter and pitch to maximize thrust efficiency, a submersible
pod electric motor for direct drive propulsion, and a custom-geared rudder system for both enhance
maneuverability and control. The power system integrates 4 LiFePO₄ and a LiPo battery, ensuring a
balance of power efficiency, safety, and redundancy.Rapid 3D: A 3D Printed Vessel 3

Background and Design Research
Pod Motors
Pod motors eliminate the need for complex gearing systems at the cost of increasing
hydrodynamic drag by being fully submerged. Research from Candela Boats highlights the efficiency
advantages of pod motor systems, demonstrating that direct-drive, water-cooled pod motors reduce
energy losses and improve overall system longevity (Candela, 2023). The C-Pod motor, for instance,
achieves near-total efficiency in power transmission by eliminating mechanical losses associated with
traditional propeller shafts (Candela, 2023). Based on these findings, the team selected the APISQUEEN
70167 E-foil motor, which shares key characteristics with high-efficiency pod motors while offering
adaptability for our specific application. In choosing APISQUEEN 70167, a submergible motor, as Rapid
3D’s motor the team eliminated the need for a complex drive shaft, and bosting 10.1 horsepower this
motor gives us more than enough power to traverse 2 miles in 50 minutes. This selection represents an
innovative departure from the conventional electric boat propulsion systems, as most existing designs rely
on a shaft system or an outboard electric motor rather than fully submerged pod systems.
Propellers
The basis of any marine propulsion system is the propeller, as it directly influences the efficiency
and thrust output of the vessel. Extensive research in marine hydrodynamics has demonstrated that
propeller diameter and pitch are key factors affecting performance (Techet, 2005). Larger-diameter
propellers generate greater thrust due to increased interaction with the surrounding water, but they also
require more torque to operate efficiently. Additionally, higher-pitch propellers improve forward
movement per rotation but can lead to cavitation if not properly optimized (Carlton, 2018). With that in
mind, the team’s research into propeller designs eventually led them to select the propeller on a Flipsky
65111. The propeller on the 65111 is configured for both torque and speed as it was designed for use on a
pod-like Efoil motor, much like ours. This was a uniquely beneficial find for the team as, utilizing another
motor’s propeller in a similar but way more powerful motor does not always turn out positively, but in the
team’s case, it did. Providing more thrust while reducing cavitations when pushing the motor to its
maximum speed.
Electrical Power System
Different types of batteries have wildly different energy densities, discharge rates, and overall
durability this is why picking the correct battery is paramount to a successful electric vessel. With that in
mind, the team investigated various battery types including lithium-ion, lithium polymer (LiPo), lithium Rapid 3D: A 3D Printed Vessel 4

iron phosphate (LiFePO₄), and even solid-state batteries. As it would turn out multiple studies indicated
that LiFePO₄ batteries offer significant advantages over other traditional lithium-ion cells. With LiFePO₄
batteries offer enhanced thermal stability, longer cycle life, and greater safety under high-current loads
(Li-Xia et al., 2011). The only other battery that would compare in its properties would be solid-state
batteries (Xiqian et al., 2023), however, due to their relatively rare and expensive nature the team decided
on LiFePO₄.
LiFePO₄ batteries are particularly suitable for electric vessels as, in a marine context, durability
and reliability far outweigh anything else. That is to say that LiFePO₄ batteries are not the ideal battery in
all contexts as they typically exhibit lower energy density compared to standard LiPo batteries, which
provide higher discharge rates but are more susceptible to thermal runaway (Xiqian et al., 2023). Given
these trade-offs, our design integrates both LiFePO₄ and LiPo batteries, with LiFePO₄ serving as the
primary energy source for propulsion and LiPo batteries supplying power to control electronics and
auxiliary systems. This unique hybrid approach maximizes energy efficiency while ensuring system
redundancy and safety as the main motor pulls from the much safer LiFePO₄ battery system while the
control electronics pull from the much more electrically dense LiPo battery.
Design and Analysis
With a drive system in mind, the team needed to create a hull capable of supporting or even
boosting the drive assembly’s performance. As the team’s budget didn’t allow for multiple hulls to be
built the initial design was paramount. In lieu of that fact, the team aimed to draw inspiration from the
hull performance of tried-and-true race boats offered by P1 Offshore, a race boat company, and first
create a model of the desired vessel in Solid Works.
Figure 2: A reference picture the team used to draw inspiration from.Rapid 3D: A 3D Printed Vessel 5

Designing the Hull
Utilizing P1’s hull design, the team began creating their own hull based upon but uniquely
different from P1’s designs. From P1’s design, the team recreated the single-hull catamaran shape of the
P1, consisting of a left and right pontoon conjoined with a midsection giving a single hull design with 2
distinct pontoons. However, modifications to P1’s designs had to be made as it could not incorporate our
drive assembly and electrical system fully.
Figure 3: The initial hull design based upon P1's
Modifications - Drive Assembly Requirements
To attach the actual drive assembly two aluminum extrusions were designed to fit into the hull
from its mating surface. The first much thicker and larger extrusion acts as a structural beam while the
second much wider but thinner extrusion acts as the actual mounting point for the drive assembly. This
second extrusion, much like the first, goes across from one hull to the next, leaving enough room for the
drive assembly in the middle to be attached using 4 bolts and locking nuts. The extrusions themselves
must mount into the hull as well so another modification to the hull was made. Two “extrusion port holes”
of differing sizes were added to both hull pontoons to accommodate the excursion, making the aluminum
extrusion the connecting piece between the left and right pontoon and the midsection. These extrusions
are friction-fitted in and then bolted in place using extrusion t-nuts and rubber-joined washers to ensure
water does not leak into the two pontoons through the mounting holes.
Figure 4: Side profile of one of the pontoons showing the cuts for the extrusions
Modifications - Electrical Requirements
After creating a system to mount the drive assembly, what came next was the electrical system.
The first thing the team did was create access hatches into the pontoons themselves after which they Rapid 3D: A 3D Printed Vessel 6

realized that the original width of P1’s design was too narrow to accommodate the size of the batteries the
drive assembly needed. After an increase in the pontoon’s width and depth the team then created a
platform and holder walls for the batteries. To keep the batteries from jumping out of the battery
compartment the team then created a simple clamp bar on top of the batteries, simply utilizing two screws
to make the bar removable.
Figure 5: Show cases the battery compartment along with the screw holes for the battery clamp
The hull can now accommodate the batteries and drive assembly, the next item on the list is the
brains of the vessel, the control electronics. To mount the control electronics the team chose to mount it
within the midsection, in between the batteries and the drive assembly, to both shorten the required cables
and to improve the center mass of the vessel. For cables to go from either pontoon to the midsection a
cable through hole was created, designed to accommodate a thick, custom, rubber O-ring to ensure that
water does not get into either the midsection or the pontoons. For extra protection against water, the
control electronics are kept within a waterproof electronics box which is then slotted and glued into the
midsection.
Figure 6: Shows the cable through Hole
As the team has chosen the FLIPSKY 75200 FOC a liquid-cooled electronic speed controller
(ESC), either a water inlet or a radiator must be mounted to the hull. The team ended up choosing to use a Rapid 3D: A 3D Printed Vessel 7

radiator as they had noticed that a water inlet is unreliable at best, due to clogging of being above the
water line, and at worst, melting from within due to its own heat. With that in mind, the team needed a
place to mount the radiator and chose the midsection as it was closest to the electrical box and allowed for
short and simple water tubing. To mount the radiator to the midsection the team created a chamber in
which the radiator is connected on the outside before being slotted in and locked into place with a
chamber cap. Within the chamber air is guided into the hull and then back out from the top, effectively
creating high airflow as the vessel picks up speed.
Figure 7: Shows the radiator chamber
Structural and Human Modifications
Once the hull design could accommodate the propulsion (drive assembly) and electrical systems
the team turned their attention to structural concerns as the hull was only ¼in thick. The team felt that
structural components were needed to ensure durability on waves and wake. The team started by creating
an endoskeleton for the pontoons, modeling structural ribs to keep the hull from collapsing inward and
creating a structural column within the hull to alleviate compressive forces caused by the bobbing motion
in water. This column also served a double purpose as it was then modified again to contain a 30lb
payload.
Figure 8: Shows the numerous structural ribs & the column
After ensuring the survivability of the hull the team then turned their attention to the human
aspects of the hull, more specifically how a human is going to pick up, lower, and generally carry the
vessel. Sitting at a 7 and ½ feet the vessel was not one that could be handled by just a single person;
therefore, the decision was made that the vessel would be handled by 4 people, resulting in 4 heavy duty Rapid 3D: A 3D Printed Vessel 8

handles being modeled and integrated into the hull to not introduce any additional air drag. The same
modeling process was then applied to the towing point conveniently located on the very tip of the
midsection.
Figure 9: shows the handles and tow point of mid-section
Assembly Modifications
Assembling a 7 and ½ feet vessel is not an easy task so the team began planning ahead on how
the hull is to be assembled. For ease of handling and construction the team decided to create the hull in
sections which brought up an issue: how would the sections line up? Trying to join multiple sections of a
7 and ½ feet free hand accurately would be an impossible task. After debating the team came up with the
novel idea to include another aluminum extrusion, which is guaranteed to be straight, within the pontoons
to act as a guide rail for the different sections. For the smaller sections and the midsection, the team
decided to create a bolt point in the middle of each structural rib enabling the section to be bolted together
before conjoining, ensuring alignment. To make assembly even easier the team also separated the
midsection into its own part. This made the hull much more transportable and created a simple modular
system in which the team could swap out either pontoons or midsection should they warrant repair or
further modifications.
Figure 10: Shows the bolt holes and internal extrusionRapid 3D: A 3D Printed Vessel 9

Analysis of the Hull
Throughout the design process, the team ensured that the model they were creating would
realistically float and effectively drive in water. They did this by running simulations and calculations
based on the model they were creating.
Calculation
Due to the hull of the vessel being modeled in solid works allowed the team to quickly calculate
the water line of the vessel and determine if the vessel would even float. The team took an absolute worstcase scenario weight of 300lb and calculated the proportional volume of water using a density of
0.037 𝑙𝑏
𝑖𝑛3
. Giving that 300lb of water has a volume of displacement of 8108.1. Relating that volume to the
model gives a water line of 6.8 inches, ensuring that the vessel will at least float
Simulation
The flow simulation done on SolidWorks works as a method of determining how efficient the
boat will perform in the water before the actual testing. To make the wizard work, a list of conditions
needed to be included. This was an external analysis that included gravity, was time-dependent, and was
free-surface. A couple of parameters were set such as velocity, 6 knots in the Z direction, and setting the
water line to be 6.8 inches. This was the estimated water line based on the Archimedes principle.
Finishing the conditions and running the wizard produces the simulated result shown below:
Figure 11: Water friction simulation done on the boat with the calculated water lineRapid 3D: A 3D Printed Vessel 10

The image shows a CFD of the boat or the Volume Fraction of Water, a visual representation of
the fluid distribution within a small domain created by the user. The legend bar corresponds to the
proportion of water in that cell. This image shows the water gathered toward the back center of the boat
due to the gap between the hulls.
Fabrication
Hull
Due to the nature of simulations and the complexities of the real world, any design of a hull will
not be one-to-one with simulations and calculations. As such the team aimed to create an optimized hull
in a way that is most reflective of simulations and calculations. Enter 3D printing, a method that allows
for a 3D model of practically anything to change from ones and zeros into a physical object one can hold
and use. With 3D printing, the team was able to replicate their exact design in the real world. This,
however, is not without its own complicated processes and decisions.
The Printer
The first decision the team had to make was on what printer would the hull be printed on. The 3D
printer the team decided on was the Neptune 4 Max by Elegoo. This decision was based on its massive
print volume (16.5×16.5×18.9in3) that was able to accommodate the sectioned portion of the hull and
midsection. On top of this, the Neptune 4 series of printers are known to be reliable, consistent, and most
importantly extremely fast, being able to print at 500 mm/s when the average 3D printer operates around
50-150 mm/s.
Material
The second decision the team had to make was on the material of the hull itself. The team
considered utilizing PLA, ASA, ABS, and other specialized plastic composites but eventually settled on
utilizing PETG. On one hand, PLA is easy to work with and print, however, it is extremely weak to heat
and doesn’t have much in terms of impact resistance on the other hand ASA and ABS are known for their
extreme durability in exterior environments, however, it is extremely hard to work with and, depending
on the material manufacturer, would produce toxic fumes while being melted by the printer (Kopar &
Yildiz, 2023). PETG is a material that is easier to work with when compared to ASA and ABS and is
known to be durable enough for exterior use (Kopar & Yildiz, 2023). To increase print times and impact Rapid 3D: A 3D Printed Vessel 11

resistance the team specifically went with Elegoo’s Rapid PETG, making the hull easier and faster to
manufacture while being more durable.
Construction
 Once all the sections of the hull are printed everything is first sanded and cleaned before being
slotted into the internal aluminum extrusion or loosely bolted together to ensure alignment. The team then
used JB Weld Plastic Bonder to permanently bond the sections together forming a uniform, 3D-printed,
hull and midsection. Once the pontoons and hull are completed the team then used heat inserts to create
secure and permanent bolt threads. This is to aid in the longevity and strength of the 3D-printed access
hatches of the hull and the battery clamp bar. Once the lids are attached and their seam taped off the team
will then use clear epoxy to coat the whole hull, utilizing fiberglass on specific stress points such as the
handles.
Figure 12: A sanded and taped off pontoon ready for epoxy
Electrical
The fabrication of the electrical system is divided into two subsystems, the High Voltage and
steering system and the low voltage control and communications system.Rapid 3D: A 3D Printed Vessel 12

Power Storage
The high voltage power storage system is constructed of four 12.8V, 100Ah LiFePO₄ batteries
connected in series, providing 51.2V for the main motor and rudder. While the low voltage system power
storage system simply consists of a 3S LiPo battery.
Figure 13: one of four 12.8V batteries
Drive Assembly - Power Train
 With 55V the team chose the APISQUEEN 70167 electric motor, a 7,500W, 10.1 HP Efoil motor
that is then attached to the Flipsky 65111 propeller. This motor assembly is then attached using two
mounting bolts and lock nuts onto the drive assembly’s aluminum extrusion. The motor assembly’s cone
is then attached on the opposite side using four standard extrusion t-nuts and M6 bolts. Two extrusions are
then attached above the motor assembly to form supports for the rutter. The rutter is then bolted onto the
90° gearbox before the gearbox and rutter supports are bolted onto the two extrusions above the motor.
This completes the drive assembly and attaching 90° brackets at the very top of the main drive assembly
extrusion finally forms the drive assembly.
Controls and Connections
 Diagrams of both the high-voltage and low-voltage systems can be found below. The team
created these diagrams and used them as a guide when putting together the systems.
The low-voltage system is contained within the electronics box. It contains the 3S LiPo which is
connected to the 12V water cooling system via a relay and to a 12V->5V buck converter. This buck
converter provides regulated 5V power to The Cube flight controller and Raspberry Pi. The GPS, Arduino
for stepper control, and RC receiver are powered by the flight controller. The PWM signal for the main Rapid 3D: A 3D Printed Vessel 13

motor and the stepper signals for the rudder control are connected from the flight controller and Arduino
to the VESC and stepper driver respectively.
The high-voltage system is connected to a bus bar to allow for easy distribution. All power from the
batteries runs through the fuse and contactor before reaching the bus bar so that the batteries are
completely cut off in the event of a power shutoff. The bus bar then provides power to the VESC and a
48V regulator to the stepper driver.
Figure 14: Electrical box wiring diagram
Testing
 Before fully assembling the boat the team actively tests the electrical components outside of the
hull to verify that they are operating nominally. The first thing the team will test is the battery’s voltage to
check for any inconsistencies that would result in damaging parts. They would do this by using a multimeter and cross-checking the result with a battery management system (BMS). The team will run
performance tests on the thrust motor under two scenarios: one that simulates the failure of the water
pump, observing how fast the ESC would heat up under different loads, and then the team would activate
the pump cooling the ESC to gauge the change in temperature. This is done in order to find the ideal
operating temperature of the ESC and the temperature that would indicate pump failure. It is also during
this test that the team will come to know the normal operational current and voltages in relation to the
amount of thrust the drive assembly produces.
Assembly
 To put the whole boat together, the team starts by grabbing either the left or right pontoon and
attaching the two connecting aluminum extrusions, locking both in place using extrusion t-nuts, rubber
bonded washers, M6, and M8 bolts. The team then grabs the radiator, connecting it’s tubing before Rapid 3D: A 3D Printed Vessel 14

inserting it into the radiator chamber and locking it in place with the radiator chamber cap. Laying the
pontoon on its side so that the extrusions are facing up, the midsection is then slid across the extrusion
until it fully presses on the pontoon, it is also then locked into place using the same method. To complete
the hull the other pontoon is slid into the extrusion and attached in the same manner as the first. To test if
the hull has been securely attached to each other two team members are asked to tug away from each
other in an attempt to separate the two pontoons and midsection.
 Now that the hull is all put together, the team inserts the four main batteries and the electrical box
into their respective compartments before securing them in place using the battery clamp bars. Cables are
then attached to the batteries and run through the “cable through” hole into the midsection and connected
to the electrical box. The team then utilized the drive assembly’s 90° bracket to bolt and lock the drive
assembly onto the middle back of the boat. After checking connections and signal, the two 30lb payloads
are then lowered into their chambers and locked into place. Once the payloads are locked in the lids are
then securely bolted into their respective locations and locked into place.
Risks
Mitigated
The team has run into a variety of risks in designing Rapid 3D especially in engineering a hull
that is to be 3D printed thankfully almost all of the risks that come with a 3D printed hull can be
mitigated. One of the biggest risks of a 3D printed hull is its durability, thankfully during the design and
build phase of the hull the team mitigated it; by designing mounting points to avoid sheering forces and
utilizing epoxy resign as both a waterproofing and strengthening agent. Another risk mitigated by epoxy
is the water resistance of a 3D printed craft, by itself 3D prints are at most water resistant and will
eventually leak but with epoxy, the team essentially completely sealed the outside of the vessel creating a
waterproof hull.
Controllable
 Although the team accounts for quite a bit of risks there are still risks when it comes to such a
unique vessel. For one due to the nature of the gearbox and how power is transferred into the rudder,
turning the vessel may result in the gears potentially skipping resulting in an offset rudder. This will cause
the vessel to start turning even though the operator is not turning. This risk can be controlled during the
race by correcting the offset values on our controller so that the vessel assumes the middle is offset by a
given angular degree.Rapid 3D: A 3D Printed Vessel 15

References
Candela. (2023, January 5). Candela Tech Talks | Episode 3, the C-Pod Motor. YouTube.
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jmaSrTV52yo
Carlton, J. (2018). Marine propellers and propulsion. Butterworth-Heinemann.
Kopar, M. & Yildiz, A. (2023). Experimental investigation of mechanical properties of PLA, ABS, and
PETG 3-d printing materials using fused deposition modeling technique. Materials Testing,
65(12), 1795-1804.
Li-Xia, Y., Zhao-Hui, W., Wu-Xing, Z., et al. (2011). Development and challenges of LiFePO4 cathode
material for lithium-ion batteries. Energy & Environmental Science.
Techet, A. H. (2005). Marine propellers and propulsion principles. Massachusetts Institute of Technology.
Workshop Insider. (2022, August 17). Guide to ships rudder and steering gear. Retrieved from
https://workshopinsider.com/ship-rudder-and-steering
Xiqian, Y., Rusong, C., Luyu, G., et al. (2023). Battery Safety: From Lithium-Ion to Solid-State Batteries.
Engineering, Volume 21, Pages 9-14

The first thing the team did was create access hatches into the pontoons themselves after which they Rapid 3D: A 3D Printed Vessel 6
realized that the original width of P1’s design was too narrow to accommodate the size of the batteries the
drive assembly needed. After an increase in the pontoon’s width and depth the team then created a
platform and holder walls for the batteries. To keep the batteries from jumping out of the battery
compartment the team then created a simple clamp bar on top of the batteries, simply utilizing two screws
to make the bar removable.
Figure 5: Show cases the battery compartment along with the screw holes for the battery clamp
The hull can now accommodate the batteries and drive assembly, the next item on the list is the
brains of the vessel, the control electronics. To mount the control electronics the team chose to mount it
within the midsection, in between the batteries and the drive assembly, to both shorten the required cables
and to improve the center mass of the vessel. For cables to go from either pontoon to the midsection a
cable through hole was created, designed to accommodate a thick, custom, rubber O-ring to ensure that
water does not get into either the midsection or the pontoons. For extra protection against water, the
control electronics are kept within a waterproof electronics box which is then slotted and glued into the
midsection.
Figure 6: Shows the cable through Hole
As the team has chosen the FLIPSKY 75200 FOC a liquid-cooled electronic speed controller
(ESC), either a water inlet or a radiator must be mounted to the hull. The team ended up choosing to use a Rapid 3D: A 3D Printed Vessel 7
radiator as they had noticed that a water inlet is unreliable at best, due to clogging of being above the
water line, and at worst, melting from within due to its own heat. With that in mind, the team needed a
place to mount the radiator and chose the midsection as it was closest to the electrical box and allowed for
short and simple water tubing. To mount the radiator to the midsection the team created a chamber in
which the radiator is connected on the outside before being slotted in and locked into place with a
chamber cap. Within the chamber air is guided into the hull and then back out from the top, effectively
creating high airflow as the vessel picks up speed.
Figure 7: Shows the radiator chamber
Structural and Human Modifications
Once the hull design could accommodate the propulsion (drive assembly) and electrical systems
the team turned their attention to structural concerns as the hull was only ¼in thick. The team felt that
structural components were needed to ensure durability on waves and wake. The team started by creating
an endoskeleton for the pontoons, modeling structural ribs to keep the hull from collapsing inward and
creating a structural column within the hull to alleviate compressive forces caused by the bobbing motion
in water. This column also served a double purpose as it was then modified again to contain a 30lb
payload.
Figure 8: Shows the numerous structural ribs & the column
After ensuring the survivability of the hull the team then turned their attention to the human
aspects of the hull, more specifically how a human is going to pick up, lower, and generally carry the
vessel. Sitting at a 7 and ½ feet the vessel was not one that could be handled by just a single person;
therefore, the decision was made that the vessel would be handled by 4 people, resulting in 4 heavy duty Rapid 3D: A 3D Printed Vessel 8
handles being modeled and integrated into the hull to not introduce any additional air drag. The same
modeling process was then applied to the towing point conveniently located on the very tip of the
midsection.
Figure 9: shows the handles and tow point of mid-section
Assembly Modifications
Assembling a 7 and ½ feet vessel is not an easy task so the team began planning ahead on how
the hull is to be assembled. For ease of handling and construction the team decided to create the hull in
sections which brought up an issue: how would the sections line up? Trying to join multiple sections of a
7 and ½ feet free hand accurately would be an impossible task. After debating the team came up with the
novel idea to include another aluminum extrusion, which is guaranteed to be straight, within the pontoons
to act as a guide rail for the different sections. For the smaller sections and the midsection, the team
decided to create a bolt point in the middle of each structural rib enabling the section to be bolted together
before conjoining, ensuring alignment. To make assembly even easier the team also separated the
midsection into its own part. This made the hull much more transportable and created a simple modular
system in which the team could swap out either pontoons or midsection should they warrant repair or
further modifications.

Analysis of the Hull
Throughout the design process, the team ensured that the model they were creating would
realistically float and effectively drive in water. They did this by running simulations and calculations
based on the model they were creating.
Calculation
Due to the hull of the vessel being modeled in solid works allowed the team to quickly calculate

the water line of the vessel and determine if the vessel would even float. The team took an absolute worstcase scenario weight of 300lb and calculated the proportional volume of water using a density of

. Giving that 300lb of water has a volume of displacement of 8108.1. Relating that volume to the
model gives a water line of 6.8 inches, ensuring that the vessel will at least float
Simulation
The flow simulation done on SolidWorks works as a method of determining how efficient the
boat will perform in the water before the actual testing. To make the wizard work, a list of conditions
needed to be included. This was an external analysis that included gravity, was time-dependent, and was
free-surface. A couple of parameters were set such as velocity, 6 knots in the Z direction, and setting the
water line to be 6.8 inches. This was the estimated water line based on the Archimedes principle.

Fabrication
Hull
Due to the nature of simulations and the complexities of the real world, any design of a hull will
not be one-to-one with simulations and calculations. As such the team aimed to create an optimized hull
in a way that is most reflective of simulations and calculations. Enter 3D printing, a method that allows
for a 3D model of practically anything to change from ones and zeros into a physical object one can hold
and use. With 3D printing, the team was able to replicate their exact design in the real world. This,
however, is not without its own complicated processes and decisions.
The Printer
The first decision the team had to make was on what printer would the hull be printed on. The 3D
printer the team decided on was the Neptune 4 Max by Elegoo. This decision was based on its massive
print volume (16.5×16.5×18.9in3) that was able to accommodate the sectioned portion of the hull and
midsection. On top of this, the Neptune 4 series of printers are known to be reliable, consistent, and most
importantly extremely fast, being able to print at 500 mm/s when the average 3D printer operates around
Material
The second decision the team had to make was on the material of the hull itself. The team
considered utilizing PLA, ASA, ABS, and other specialized plastic composites but eventually settled on
utilizing PETG. On one hand, PLA is easy to work with and print, however, it is extremely weak to heat
and doesn’t have much in terms of impact resistance on the other hand ASA and ABS are known for their
extreme durability in exterior environments, however, it is extremely hard to work with and, depending
on the material manufacturer, would produce toxic fumes while being melted by the printer (Kopar &
Yildiz, 2023). PETG is a material that is easier to work with when compared to ASA and ABS and is
known to be durable enough for exterior use (Kopar & Yildiz, 2023). To increase print times and impact Rapid 3D: A 3D Printed Vessel 11
resistance the team specifically went with Elegoo’s Rapid PETG, making the hull easier and faster to
manufacture while being more durable.
Construction
Once all the sections of the hull are printed everything is first sanded and cleaned before being
slotted into the internal aluminum extrusion or loosely bolted together to ensure alignment. The team then
used JB Weld Plastic Bonder to permanently bond the sections together forming a uniform, 3D-printed,
hull and midsection. Once the pontoons and hull are completed the team then used heat inserts to create
secure and permanent bolt threads. This is to aid in the longevity and strength of the 3D-printed access
hatches of the hull and the battery clamp bar. Once the lids are attached and their seam taped off the team
will then use clear epoxy to coat the whole hull, utilizing fiberglass on specific stress points such as the
handles.
Figure 12: A sanded and taped off pontoon ready for epoxy
Electrical
The fabrication of the electrical system is divided into two subsystems, the High Voltage and
steering system and the low voltage control and communications system.Rapid 3D: A 3D Printed Vessel 12
Power Storage
The high voltage power storage system is constructed of four 12.8V, 100Ah LiFePO₄ batteries
connected in series, providing 51.2V for the main motor and rudder. While the low voltage system power
storage system simply consists of a 3S LiPo battery.
Figure 13: one of four 12.8V batteries
Drive Assembly - Power Train
With 55V the team chose the APISQUEEN 70167 electric motor, a 7,500W, 10.1 HP Efoil motor
that is then attached to the Flipsky 65111 propeller. This motor assembly is then attached using two
mounting bolts and lock nuts onto the drive assembly’s aluminum extrusion. The motor assembly’s cone
is then attached on the opposite side using four standard extrusion t-nuts and M6 bolts. Two extrusions are
then attached above the motor assembly to form supports for the rutter. The rutter is then bolted onto the
90° gearbox before the gearbox and rutter supports are bolted onto the two extrusions above the motor.
This completes the drive assembly and attaching 90° brackets at the very top of the main drive assembly
extrusion finally forms the drive assembly.
Controls and Connections
Diagrams of both the high-voltage and low-voltage systems can be found below. The team
created these diagrams and used them as a guide when putting together the systems.
The low-voltage system is contained within the electronics box. It contains the 3S LiPo which is
connected to the 12V water cooling system via a relay and to a 12V->5V buck converter. This buck
converter provides regulated 5V power to The Cube flight controller and Raspberry Pi. The GPS, Arduino
for stepper control, and RC receiver are powered by the flight controller. The PWM signal for the main Rapid 3D: A 3D Printed Vessel 13
motor and the stepper signals for the rudder control are connected from the flight controller and Arduino
to the VESC and stepper driver respectively.
The high-voltage system is connected to a bus bar to allow for easy distribution. All power from the
batteries runs through the fuse and contactor before reaching the bus bar so that the batteries are
completely cut off in the event of a power shutoff. The bus bar then provides power to the VESC and a
48V regulator to the stepper driver.
Figure 14: Electrical box wiring diagram
Testing
Before fully assembling the boat the team actively tests the electrical components outside of the
hull to verify that they are operating nominally. The first thing the team will test is the battery’s voltage to
check for any inconsistencies that would result in damaging parts. They would do this by using a multimeter and cross-checking the result with a battery management system (BMS). The team will run
performance tests on the thrust motor under two scenarios: one that simulates the failure of the water
pump, observing how fast the ESC would heat up under different loads, and then the team would activate
the pump cooling the ESC to gauge the change in temperature. This is done in order to find the ideal
operating temperature of the ESC and the temperature that would indicate pump failure. It is also during
this test that the team will come to know the normal operational current and voltages in relation to the
amount of thrust the drive assembly produces.
Assembly
To put the whole boat together, the team starts by grabbing either the left or right pontoon and
attaching the two connecting aluminum extrusions, locking both in place using extrusion t-nuts, rubber
bonded washers, M6, and M8 bolts. The team then grabs the radiator, connecting it’s tubing before Rapid 3D: A 3D Printed Vessel 14
inserting it into the radiator chamber and locking it in place with the radiator chamber cap. Laying the
pontoon on its side so that the extrusions are facing up, the midsection is then slid across the extrusion
until it fully presses on the pontoon, it is also then locked into place using the same method. To complete
the hull the other pontoon is slid into the extrusion and attached in the same manner as the first. To test if
the hull has been securely attached to each other two team members are asked to tug away from each
other in an attempt to separate the two pontoons and midsection.
Now that the hull is all put together, the team inserts the four main batteries and the electrical box
into their respective compartments before securing them in place using the battery clamp bars. Cables are
then attached to the batteries and run through the “cable through” hole into the midsection and connected
to the electrical box. The team then utilized the drive assembly’s 90° bracket to bolt and lock the drive
assembly onto the middle back of the boat. After checking connections and signal, the two 30lb payloads
are then lowered into their chambers and locked into place. Once the payloads are locked in the lids are
then securely bolted into their respective locations and locked into place.
Risks
Mitigated
The team has run into a variety of risks in designing Rapid 3D especially in engineering a hull
that is to be 3D printed thankfully almost all of the risks that come with a 3D printed hull can be
mitigated. One of the biggest risks of a 3D printed hull is its durability, thankfully during the design and
build phase of the hull the team mitigated it; by designing mounting points to avoid sheering forces and
utilizing epoxy resign as both a waterproofing and strengthening agent. Another risk mitigated by epoxy
is the water resistance of a 3D printed craft, by itself 3D prints are at most water resistant and will
eventually leak but with epoxy, the team essentially completely sealed the outside of the vessel creating a
waterproof hull.
Controllable
Although the team accounts for quite a bit of risks there are still risks when it comes to such a
unique vessel. For one due to the nature of the gearbox and how power is transferred into the rudder,
turning the vessel may result in the gears potentially skipping resulting in an offset rudder. This will cause
the vessel to start turning even though the operator is not turning. This risk can be controlled during the
race by correcting the offset values on our controller so that the vessel assumes the middle is offset by a
given angular degree.Rapid 3D: A 3D Printed Vessel 15
